The PWA 1480E superalloy consists of about 40% gamma (γ) matrix and 60% gamma prime (γ') precipitates.
The cuboidal γ' precipitates are surrounded by the γ matrix network, and the material also contains large particles of carbides (2-3% by volume) and a small number of voids and oxide inclusions.

Tensile testing of PWA 1480E single crystals in a helium atmosphere at room temperature showed that the [110] oriented specimen exhibited the maximum tensile strength, while the [100] oriented specimen was the weakest.

TEM studies revealed that the deformation in the PWA 1480E single crystals occurred inhomogeneously in intense slip bands lying on (111) planes, and dislocation accumulations were detected within the narrow γ regions and near the γ/γ' interfaces.

In the hydrogen environment at room temperature, all the PWA 1480E single crystal specimens failed predominantly by (100) type cleavage, in contrast to the (111) type cleavage observed in the helium environment.
The tensile strength degradation in hydrogen was anisotropic, with the [100] oriented specimen exhibiting the greatest strength degradation, while the [111] oriented specimen was the strongest.
At 871°C, the specimens tested in helium failed predominantly by (111) type cleavage, with the [100] oriented specimen having the highest strength and the [110] oriented specimen being the weakest.

In hydrogen at 871°C, all the PWA 1480E single crystal specimens possessed very nearly the same tensile strength and failed predominantly by (111) type cleavage, similar to the behavior in helium at the same temperature.
The presence of (100) type cleavage in the hydrogen-charged [100] specimen near the notch root was suggested to be the reason for the largest strength degradation in this orientation.
TEM studies indicated that hydrogen enhanced dislocation accumulation in the γ region and microcracking along the (100) γ/γ' interfaces were observed in the area near the fractured surface.
